pending_articles.title: Separation, isolation, and membrane lipid profiling of selectively vulnerable and resilient neurons
pending_articles.content: Certain neurons are more susceptible to pathogenic stressors and degenerate, while others remain resilient in neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this cell-to-cell heterogeneity in neuronal vulnerability remain unclear, primarily due to challenges in isolating vulnerable and resilient neurons to characterize their properties. In this study, we report the development of a novel cell-labeling method utilizing two cell-impermeable dyes to identify vulnerable and resilient neurons in culture, which are subsequently separated and isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). As a proof-of-concept of a mechanistic study, we conducted lipidomic analysis to determine whether the lipid composition of membranes differs between vulnerable and resilient neurons to oxidative stress. This simple but unique method sets the groundwork for investigating the molecular underpinnings of selective neuronal vulnerability, which could inform new diagnostic strategies and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

pending_articles.title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During Inflammation
pending_articles.content: Background: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-{gamma} receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods: We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results: At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst (p=0.0006), neuropeptide Y (Npy) (p=0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) (p<0.0001), and synapsin 1 (Syn1) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Aif1, encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions: IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.

pending_articles.title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
pending_articles.content: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). We tested how impaired Mg2+ block at GluN1/GluN2A receptors mutated at the GluN2A-N615 position modifies inhibition by dizocilpine-derived K2060 compared with clinically used memantine and ketamine. Experimental Approach: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on recombinant wild-type (WT) and mutated GluN1/GluN2A receptors expressed in HEK293T cells. Acute hippocampal slice electrophysiology and behavioural studies were conducted in WT and knock-in GluN2A-N615S mice. In vivo tolerability and efficacy were evaluated using open field testing, prepulse inhibition (PPI), and protection against audiogenic seizures (AGS). Key Results: Mg2+ reduced the apparent potency of all three blockers and slowed onset at the GluN1/GluN2A-WT receptor. These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. In vivo, K2060 caused no overt behavioural disruption at 5 mg/kg (i.p.) and did not further disrupt PPI. All three blockers protected GluN2A-N615S mice against AGS at 5 mg/kg (i.p.); only K2060 remained protective at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Additional pharmacokinetic, safety, and disease-model studies are warranted.

pending_articles.title: Exploratory Proteomics of Brain Extracellular Vesicle Enriched Preparations After LPS Challenge and miRNA Associated Vesicle Administration
pending_articles.content: We used brain extracellular vesicle (EV) proteomics to identify protein responses to acute neuroinflammation and an EV-based microRNA intervention. Rats received vehicle, intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS), or LPS followed by an intravenous EV formulation containing anti-inflammatory microRNAs (miRNAs). Brains were collected 24 h after LPS or vehicle administration, and three independently processed animal-derived EV-enriched preparations per group were analyzed by label-free proteomics. Across all nine samples, 953 protein groups had complete normalized abundance measurements. Compared with vehicle controls, LPS exposure was associated with 227 exploratory protein changes, comprising 95 increases and 132 decreases at nominal P < 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change >= log2(1.5). Increased proteins were enriched for translation-related annotations, whereas decreased proteins were enriched for plasma-membrane annotations. These LPS-associated changes did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q < 0.05. Following treatment, 119 of the 227 candidates were closer to control abundance on the log2 scale; 23 candidates also showed nominal treatment-versus-LPS differences. Lamb2 and Ptgfrn were the two proteins that differed significantly between treated and LPS-only animals after FDR correction, identifying them as priorities for further validation. Nevertheless, 174 proteins differed significantly between treated animals and vehicle controls, and analysis across the measured proteins did not demonstrate an overall shift toward control values. Thus, the intervention was associated with specific protein responses, but treated animals retained substantial differences from controls. This study identifies candidate markers for investigating treatment responses in brain EV-enriched preparations and demonstrates the value of examining individual proteins alongside broader proteomic changes. Independent validation is needed to determine their functional relevance and distinguish miRNA-specific effects from contributions of the administered EV carrier.

pending_articles.title: Intrastriatal injection of amplified Lewy body dementia (LBD) fibrils in mice results in accumulation of fibrils with LBD structure and neurodegeneration
pending_articles.content: The defining neuropathologic feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) is alpha-synuclein (Asyn) fibril accumulation in Lewy bodies (LBs) and Lewy neurites (LNs). Recently, we developed a method to amplify Asyn fibrils derived from human post-mortem LBD brain tissue and determined that the structure of amplified Asyn fibrils is highly similar to the structure of fibrils directly isolated from LBD brain tissue. We examined whether injection of these fibrils into humanized Asyn mice recapitulates pathologic Asyn fibril accumulation with human LBD Asyn fibril structure. We utilized mice containing a null allele in the mouse Snca gene and a human SNCA transgene. Intrastriatal injection of amplified Asyn fibrils derived from 3 different LBD autopsy cases resulted in cytoplasmic and neuritic phospho-Asyn accumulation in the striatum, cortex, and amygdala bilaterally at 3mpi. Fibril injections produced a reduction in the number of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, with LB-like inclusions in surviving neurons, and produced impaired sensorimotor function as measured on the accelerating rotarod test. Fibril accumulation increased 3.6-fold between 1 and 3 months post-injection (mpi) and was relatively stable between 3 and 5 mpi. We amplified fibrils from mouse brain tissue 5 mpi and collected single-particle cryo-EM data. High resolution 3D structural information could not be obtained because of the lack of helical twist, but comparison of the cryo-EM 2D class averages with those derived from amplified fibrils prepared from human LBD tissue revealed multiple matching classes, indicating that the Lewy fold is maintained in the fibrils that accumulate in mouse brain tissue. Our findings demonstrate an approach to model the accumulation of Asyn fibrils with LBD structure in mice, providing a platform for investigating disease mechanisms, imaging biomarkers, and therapeutics targeting Asyn in PD/LBD.

pending_articles.title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia activates microglia to promote satiety via an ASC dependent signaling.
pending_articles.content: Reactive microglia are commonly considered neurotoxic and detrimental for brain functioning. Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet strongly activates microglia, disrupts the central control of energy metabolism, contributes to obesity, and promotes cognitive decline. In this study we report an unexpected beneficial function of microglia reaction at the time scale of a meal, whereby they promote satiety in a macronutrient-dependent manner. We show that murine microglia react to ingested dietary fat within three hours. Specifically, postprandial hypertriglyceridemia induced microglial hyper-ramification alongside with a transcriptional reprogramming promoting communication with neurons. This effect occurs in discrete brain areas, including the hypothalamus and the brainstem, which control hunger. Remarkably, microglia-specific genetic ablation of Apoptosis-associated Speck-like protein containing a CARD (named ASC), a master regulator of metabolism, immune function and cell shape, profoundly alters satiety following high-fat food consumption. These results reveal that microglia engage an immune signaling pathway to rapidly alert the neural circuits and activate an anorectic response that limits overconsumption of dietary fat. Unexpectedly, this regulatory process is sexually dimorphic, present in males only. Furthermore, we found that the postprandial microglial reaction is bypassed during obesity, providing a new therapeutic target to treat maladaptive eating disorders.

recently_processed.title: Decoding Spikes From Multiunit Data
recently_processed.content: Communication and control in biological systems is mediated by the timing of discharges –spikes– from excitable cells such as neurons and muscle fibers. Each spike is associated to a characteristic waveform that can be captured by sensors. The waveform's characteristics depend on the cell's biophysical properties and the recording modality. Depending on the technique, e.g., electrical recordings with electrodes, optical imaging, ultrasound, the observed signals are mixtures of waveforms emitted from active cells/sources (multiunit data/signals). Recovering the timing and identity of these sources (multiunit or spike decoding) is central to neuroscience, clinical diagnostics, and neural interfacing, yet it remains challenging due to waveform superposition, non-stationarity, limited training labels, and the computational demands of high-density recordings. This review provides a unified methodological perspective on spike decoding by formalizing the problem as a sparse source separation task under a convolutive mixing model. Rather than organizing the literature by application domain, we group and critically compare methods by their underlying principles: classical spike sorting, Bayesian and probabilistic inference, blind source separation, and data-driven approaches, including deep learning and hybrid schemes. For each class of methods, we present the core mathematical formulation and algorithmic strategies and discuss assumptions and limitations. Our synthesis highlights parallels in signal processing across physical recording modalities and clarifies when and why particular approaches succeed or fail. By bridging previously compartmentalized literature, this survey aims to accelerate crosspollination of ideas between application areas and to provide a roadmap for selecting, adapting, and advancing decoding methods across diverse multiunit recording modalities.

recently_processed.title: Intersectional genetic targeting of molecularly distinct melanin-concentrating hormone neuron subpopulations reveals distinct and overlapping subcircuit architecture
recently_processed.content: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) coordinates crucial and innate behaviors through heterogeneous yet poorly understood neuronal populations and circuits. Neurons that produce melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH; encoded by the Pmch gene) are primarily localized in the LHA and contribute to feeding, sleep-wake regulation, memory, and reward-associated behaviors. Building on foundational anatomical studies, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the LHA identified markers distinguishing at least two transcriptionally distinct MCH subpopulations. These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We hypothesized that MCH neurons operate through functionally distinct, parallel subcircuits that exhibit unique neuroanatomical projections. In this study, we leveraged Pmch and Tacr3 expression to intersectionally dissociate these neurons into Type I MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3+) and Type II MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3-) subpopulations. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Overall, these data establish the first subpopulation-resolved anatomical framework for molecularly distinct Type I and Type II MCH subcircuits, thus establishing a foundation for future circuit-level functional studies.

recently_processed.title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
recently_processed.content: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.

recently_processed.title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
recently_processed.content: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.
